transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-07
Start time: 08:42 UTC
Duration: 65 minutes
Attendees: Ari Nguyen, Samira Patel, Jordan Lee, Priya Kapoor (Redwood) — Carlos Vega, Maya Singh, Evan Roberts, Jin Park (Luminex)

[00:00] Ari: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — Ari from Redwood, Samira and Jordan on the technical side. Carlos, Maya, Evan, Jin, you there?
[00:06] Carlos: Yeah, here. Morning. Sorry am on weird connection — I'll try to keep audio ok.
[00:11] Maya: Morning all. Carlos had asked us to focus this on the SLA and noisy neighbor risk — we run critical triage workflows so p95 latency is a hard req.
[00:19] Ari: Great, that's exactly what we want to dig into. Samira, want to kick off with the isolation overview?
[00:24] Samira: Sure. So high level, we offer two relevant patterns — dedicated capacity which is fenced GPU pools you reserve, and hosted multi-tenant where we autoscale across customers. Dedicated gives you strict throughput guarantees because we carve out machines and scheduling. Hosted is more elastic but there's potential noisy neighbor effects under heavy bursts.
[00:40] Maya: When you say carve out, is that at the GPU level or node level? We care about noisy neighbor causing memory pressure and eviction.
[00:46] Samira: We do node-level isolation for dedicated, and can optionally reserve full GPU instances per customer. For most enterprise plans we do capacity pools that get pined to your tenancy — that ensures KV cache and GPU memory are not shared. There are still host-level daemons but user workloads are containerized and resource-limited.
[01:03] Jin: So in practice that means our KV cache never gets evicted by another tenant?
[01:07] Samira: Correct, within dedicated pools the prefix/KV cache lives on the same reserved instances. You can configure cache size — e.g., 40GB, 80GB — and eviction policy. Noisy neighbor cache thrash from other customers shouldn't happen. In hosted we do per-tenant logical namespaces but physical memory can be shared, so eviction is possible.
[01:26] Evan: How about CPU side buddies — I/O spikes from other tenants clogging NVMe?
[01:30] Jordan: We offer I/O QoS at the node level in Dedicated — IO throttling and separate NVMe partitions if needed. For strict cases we can provision separate disks.
[01:38] Carlos: Ok. Let's talk latency — we need p95 < 180ms for our triage use case at steady state, and p99 under 400ms. Can Dedicated guarantee that?
[01:47] Samira: We target per-token generation latency and tail latency using a combination of pre-warmed instances, bounded batching, and KV cache warmup. For Dedicated, with pre-warm and zero cold starts, p95 at your median sequence length (you'll have to send traces) is usually achievable. But p99 depends on workload spikes and sequence length outliers — that's where fallback policies help.
[02:07] Maya: We will send traces. Typical prompt + context is about 1.2k tokens, ~512 expected generation tokens for the triage summarizer.
[02:14] Jordan: That sequence length matters a lot. Longer contexts increase KV lookup and KV cache effectiveness, but also make batching windows more complex.
[02:22] Ari: On batching — quick overview: we use continuous batching with adaptive windows. We attempt to batch up to X concurrent requests based on latency headroom. If you need strict p95, we cap batching windows smaller which increases GPU utilization cost.
[02:37] Maya: So there's a cost/latency tradeoff. Can you give ballpark numbers for increased cost if we force tight windows?
[02:42] Samira: Roughly, capping batch windows to keep p95 low might increase per-token cost by 15–35% depending on model and qps. We can run benchmark with your traces to quantify.
[02:53] Jin: What about the KV cache hit rate — what's realistic? If our contexts are highly repetitive (same patient meta fields) I'd expect high hit rate, but if not, eviction thrash could kill performance.
[03:04] Jordan: Typical hit rates range 40–85% depending on prompt reuse. For a triage pipeline with repeated templates we often see 60–75% hits. Samira will size cache recommendations based on your traces.
[03:17] Carlos: Quantization — we're concerned about hallucinations introduced by aggressive 4-bit quantization. Does Redwood support mixed quantization strategies?
[03:23] Samira: Yes. We support per-layer mixed quantization profiles and int8/4-bit variants. Our runtime has quality monitors — we can route a percentage of requests to full precision for A/B quality sampling. For mission-critical outputs you can pin model type and disable aggressive quant. That impacts throughput — 4-bit often gives 1.6–2x throughput uplift but can degrade certain generations.
[03:44] Evan: How do you validate quality regressions? We need an eval harness that compares outputs against golden prompts.
[03:49] Priya: Redwood Optimize has a quality monitoring pipeline; we can ingest your prompt set and run regression alerts. We'll propose a sampling plan during pilot.
[03:58] Maya: Back to failover — say a GPU node fails, what's the failover path and effect on in-flight requests?
[04:03] Samira: In Dedicated we replicate KV shards across a hot-standby within the same region so failover is fast — we lose some in-flight latency but not the entire cache. For strict SLOs we recommend a primary+hot standby pair per critical pool.
[04:15] Jordan: For in-flight requests, our runtime can checkpoint KV state and replay on failover, but that adds a few hundred milliseconds for recovery. We typically set graceful degradation: fallback to smaller model with warm cache or reduce max tokens.
[04:28] Carlos: That leads to behavioral differences — returning shorter summaries on failover is acceptable as long as we know. Can Redwood surface reasons for degraded output to downstream?
[04:34] Priya: Yes — the Console surfaces automatic fallback events, model variant used, and a reason code (e.g., NODE_FAIL, CAPACITY_FALLBACK, QUANTIZED_VARIANT). Those are included in logs and traces.
[04:44] Jin: Networking — for VPC private deployments, what's the latency impact for peered traffic? We plan to peer via AWS Transit Gateway across accounts.
[04:52] Samira: If the control plane is in Redwood-managed VPC and you peer, typical extra RTT is small — <5ms regionally. For on-prem air-gapped setups, if inference happens on-prem we eliminate extra network RTTs. However, on-prem adds ops burden and patching windows.
[05:07] Evan: Security: KMS/HSM support, audit logs, and SSO were all mentioned in your SOC2 docs — can you provide the runbook for KMS rotation?
[05:14] Ari: We'll send the KMS integration guide. We support customer-managed keys in both Hosted and Dedicated; for Private on-prem we support HSM by request.
[05:21] Maya: Ok good. A question on throughput guarantees: if we sign Reserved Dedicated capacity with a QPS commit, what happens if demand spikes above the contract?
[05:29] Samira: Reserved gives you baseline capacity. For spikes, you have two levers: burst capacity (paid overage) which uses spare pool and has a priority bump, or graceful fallback to smaller model/region. We can also set automatic routing to Hosted overflow but that's risky for data residency.
[05:45] Carlos: We don't want our PII to cross into multi-tenant Hosted. So overflow to Hosted is not allowed.
[05:50] Ari: We can set hard limits — no overflow — and instead trigger throttling or preconfigured fallback. That will be part of the SLA.
[05:58] Jin: How about noisy neighbor in Hosted — can you throttle other tenants?
[06:02] Jordan: In Hosted we do scheduling priority and fairness but you can still see interference under extreme conditions. We recommend dedicated for strict p95 SLOs.
[06:11] Evan: For the pilot, we want to run synthetic and replayed traffic. How do we emulate cold/warm cache states?
[06:17] Samira: We'll set up two phases — phase A warm (seed cache with traces) and phase B cold (flush cache between runs). We'll measure p50/p95/p99, hit rates, and CPU/GPU utilization.
[06:26] Maya: Can you also show impact of quantization toggles during the pilot?
[06:29] Priya: Yes — we'll include A/B with mixed quant profiles and sample quality comparisons.
[06:33] Carlos: A few nitty gritty: what's your KV eviction policy? LRU, segmented-LRU, or TTL-based?
[06:39] Jordan: Default is an adaptive LRU with TTL shards for time-bounded keys. For your use-case we might recommend TTL + frequency weighting because templates are stable but user-specific context is ephemeral.
[06:49] Jin: Disk persistence — do you persist KV to NVMe across restarts?
[06:53] Samira: Yes, persistent checkpointing to instance storage with async replication. For Dedicated we can use provisioned NVMe; for Hosted it's multi-tenant SSDs.
[06:59] Evan: Auditability — can we pull an event stream of fallback events and model variant choices?
[07:05] Priya: Absolutely; Console exposes events via webhook or S3 log exports. We'll provide a sample schema.
[07:12] Carlos: Any gotchas on model tokenization differences across quantized variants? We hit a few places where token alignments change behavior.
[07:18] Samira: Tokenization is model-level; quant doesn't change tokenization. But generation behavior can change slightly — token probs shift. That's why we recommend a golden-prompt regression test in Optimize.
[07:28] Maya: In terms of numbers, can you give a rough throughput bound per GPU for our target model family?
[07:33] Jordan: Without exact model name it's rough, but for a 70B-ish open model at int8 on A100-class hardware you might get ~60–80 tokens/sec per GPU with batching; 4-bit could push to 110–140 tokens/sec. Those numbers vary with sequence lengths and KV usage.
[07:50] Carlos: Perfect. Let's talk SLAs in writing — uptime, latency SLOs, and remedies.
[07:56] Ari: We'll draft SLA language: baseline uptime 99.95% for Dedicated, latency SLOs tied to pilot medians (e.g., p95 <= 180ms) with credits for missed SLOs. We'll include definitions for force-majeure, maintenance windows, and failover behaviors.
[08:11] Evan: We need a clause about no automatic overflow to multi-tenant and proof of isolation for Dedicated.
[08:16] Ari: Noted — we will provide isolation evidence: topology diagrams, tenant allocation snapshots, and sample logging that shows no cross-tenant KV collisions.
[08:24] Maya: One more ops question — what timescale for scaling capacity? If we hit sustained higher qps, how fast can Redwood add more dedicated nodes?
[08:30] Samira: With reserved commitments we can schedule capacity within 48–72 hours for predicted increases. For urgent temporary increases, burst capacity can be enabled within minutes if available in region.
[08:40] Carlos: Ok that aligns with our RTO requirements.
[08:44] Ari: Let's recap next steps quickly. We will send the dedicated config, SLA draft, KMS guide, and sample pilot plan. Luminex will send traces and security constraints. Samira will size cache and propose quant/batching defaults.
[08:56] Maya: Sounds good. Any other questions?
[09:00] Evan: One small ask — can you include a fallback policy example in the runbook with exact thresholds (e.g., p95 > 300ms triggers fallback to small-model at 20% traffic)?
[09:08] Priya: Yes we'll provide example policies and a suggested threshold matrix.
[09:12] Carlos: Great. If there's nothing else we'll end here. Thanks team.
[09:16] Ari: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with artifacts.
[09:19] Maya: Thanks.

Post-meeting notes:
- Redwood to avoid default overflow to Hosted without explicit permission from Luminex.
- Pilot plan will have warm and cold phases plus quant A/B.
- Security to review KMS and VPC runbooks offline.
- Redwood suggested model pinning for top-of-pipeline triage to avoid silent degradation.

Transcript quirks: occasional partial words from Carlos due to low uplink, some proper nouns (model names) were generalized by recorder (e.g., "70B-ish" recorded as "70 Bish"), speaker overlaps at ~06:00 timestamp.
